simulation-s1.title: Simulated families collecting 4 prizes
simulation-s1.text: Each box of a cereal holds one of 4 prizes, and each prize is in one fourth of the boxes, packed at random. A student used random numbers to simulate 100 families, each buying boxes until it had all 4 prizes. Each dot shows how many boxes one simulated family bought.

plot.label: Dotplot of the number of boxes bought by 100 simulated families until they had all 4 prizes, from 4 to 18 boxes
plot.xLabel: Number of boxes bought to get all 4 prizes

simulation-s2.title: Simulating free throws with random digits
simulation-s2.text: A basketball player makes 70% of her free throws. A coach wants to estimate the chance that she makes 9 or more of her next 10 free throws, and plans a simulation with a table of random digits (each digit from 0 to 9 is as likely as the others).

items.q: Use the simulation to estimate the chance that a family needs 10 or more boxes to get all 4 prizes.

why.correct: Count the dots at 10 or more: 27 of the 100 trials. The estimate is $\frac{27}{100} = 0.27$.

mistakes.why: That counts only the trials above 10. "10 or more" includes the trials at exactly 10.
That is the share of trials that needed 9 or fewer boxes, the other side.

items.q: What does one dot in the dotplot stand for?

why.correct: Each dot is one trial: one simulated family buying boxes until all 4 prizes appear, recorded as the number of boxes.
options: Each dot is a whole run of boxes, not a single box.
The dots stack by number of boxes bought, not by prize.
The families were simulated with random numbers; no one was surveyed.
Right: the result of one repetition of the chance process.
One box of cereal opened by the student who ran the simulation
One of the 4 prizes, with its count of boxes stacked above it
One real family surveyed in a store about how many boxes it bought
One trial: a simulated family buying boxes until it has all 4 prizes

items.q: Estimate the chance that a family gets all 4 prizes in the first 4 boxes.

why.correct: 9 of the 100 simulated families needed exactly 4 boxes, so the estimate is $\frac{9}{100} = 0.09$.

mistakes.why: That is the chance for one box to hold one particular prize. Getting 4 different prizes in 4 boxes is much less likely; count the dots at 4.
That uses the number of boxes, 4, as a count of trials. Count how many dots sit at 4.

items.q: A family bought 15 boxes before it found all 4 prizes. Based on the simulation, is that surprising?

why.correct: Only 3 of the 100 simulated families needed 15 or more boxes, an estimated chance of about 0.03. That is unusual, but it does happen when prizes are packed at random.
options: The most common results being near 6 or 7 is the reason 15 is unusual, not typical.
Right: an estimated chance of about 0.03, rare but not impossible.
Some simulated families needed 15 or more boxes, up to 18.
A simulation built from the right chance process is exactly how to judge it.
No: the most common results are near 6 or 7 boxes, so 15 is typical
Somewhat: about 3 in 100 simulated families needed 15 or more boxes
Yes: no simulated family needed more than 12 boxes
It is impossible to judge, because the simulation used random numbers

items.q: How could the student get a more trustworthy estimate of the chance of needing 10 or more boxes?

why.correct: By the law of large numbers, the share of trials with the result settles down near the true value as the number of trials grows.
options: Choosing the larger estimate builds in a bias toward larger values.
The model has to match the real packing, one fourth for each prize.
Right: more trials give a steadier estimate.
Stopping early changes what is being simulated and hides the long runs.
Run the same 100 trials again and keep whichever estimate is larger
Change the prize chances so that 10 boxes is the most common result
Run many more trials, such as 1,000 simulated families
Stop each trial after 9 boxes so that the results are closer together

items.q: Which assignment of digits models one free throw correctly?

why.correct: Seven of the ten digits must mean a make: 0 to 6 is 7 digits (70%), 7 to 9 is 3 digits (30%).
options: That reverses the plan: makes get 3 of the 10 digits, a 30% chance.
That is 8 of the 10 digits, an 80% chance of a make.
That is 5 of the 10 digits, a 50% chance, not 70%.
Right: 7 of the 10 equally common digits, 70%.
Digits 0 to 6 mean a miss; digits 7 to 9 mean a make
Digits 0 to 7 mean a make; digits 8 and 9 mean a miss
Digits 0 to 4 mean a make; digits 5 to 9 mean a miss
Digits 0 to 6 mean a make; digits 7 to 9 mean a miss

items.q: In this simulation, what is one trial?

why.correct: One trial must copy the whole situation once: 10 free throws, so 10 random digits, recording the number of makes.
options: Right: one trial imitates the 10 free throws once.
One digit is one shot; the question is about 10 shots together.
The player takes 10 shots; 9 is the result being counted.
The 70% decides which digits are makes, not how many digits to use.
A group of 10 random digits, recording how many of them are makes
One random digit, recording whether it is a make or a miss
A group of 9 random digits, since the question asks about 9 makes
A group of 70 random digits, one for each percent of her makes

items.q: Should the coach skip a digit that repeats one already used in the same trial?

why.correct: Each shot has the same 70% chance whatever happened on earlier shots, so repeated digits are kept. Skipping repeats is for choosing different individuals, such as people for a sample.
options: Skipping repeats is for selecting different individuals, like a sample of students.
Right: shots are not people being chosen, so repeats are fine.
Keeping repeats is what keeps every shot at 70%; skipping them would distort the chances.
Every digit is assigned; 0 is one of the make digits in the 0 to 6 plan.
Yes: a digit used once has already been chosen and should be skipped
No: each shot has the same 70% chance whatever happened before
Yes: repeated digits would make the estimate too high
No: but she should skip 0, since 0 is neither a make nor a miss

items.q: Using digits 0 to 6 for a make, how many makes are in the row of digits shown?

why.correct: The digits 4, 0, 2, 1, 6, 3 and 5 are makes (7 of them); 8, 7 and 9 are misses. This trial is a 7, so it does not count as "9 or more".

mistakes.why: That counts the misses (8, 7, 9). Count the digits from 0 to 6.
Check again: 4, 0, 2, 1, 6, 3 and 5 are all from 0 to 6, which is 7 makes.

items.q: What is a simulation in statistics?

why.correct: A simulation imitates a chance process with a model (random numbers, a coin, a spinner) that has the same chances, repeated many times to estimate how often a result happens.
options: A simulation uses a model of the chance process, not real subjects.
That is a sample survey. A simulation imitates chance with a model.
A simulation produces data from a model; it is not a guess.
Right: then the share of trials with the result estimates its chance.
Repeating a real experiment on people until the result is clear
Collecting a random sample from a population and computing a statistic
Guessing a likely result from experience before collecting any data
Imitating a chance process with a model that has the same chances, many times

items.q: A fair coin lands heads in 13 of its first 20 flips (0.65). After 2,000 flips, the share of heads is most likely to be

why.correct: The law of large numbers: in many trials the share of heads settles near the true value, 0.5. Early streaks are not "made up for"; they are swamped by later flips.
options: Right: the long-run share approaches the true chance.
The first 20 flips carry little weight among 2,000.
The coin does not remember; the early surplus is diluted, not reversed.
For a fair coin, the long-run share is near 0.5.
close to 0.5
close to 0.65
below 0.5, to balance the early heads
impossible to guess from what is known

items.q: Two students simulate the same chance process. One runs 50 trials and estimates 0.12; the other runs 1,000 trials and estimates 0.09. Which estimate is more trustworthy, and why?

why.correct: Estimates from more trials vary less around the true value (the law of large numbers), so 0.09 from 1,000 trials is more trustworthy.
options: A larger estimate is not a better one.
Right: 1,000 trials give a steadier estimate than 50.
The model is the same, but 50 trials leave much more room for chance.
Simulations vary by chance; more trials reduce that variation.
0.12, because the first student got a larger share of successes
0.09, because estimates from more trials stay closer to the true value
Each is equally trustworthy, since both used the same model
Neither one, because two simulations should give the same answer

items.q: To study families with 4 children, a student simulates 200 families, using a coin flip for each child (heads for a girl). In 46 of the 200 simulated families, 3 or more of the children were girls. Estimate the chance that a family of 4 children has 3 or more girls.

why.correct: The estimate is the share of trials with the result: $\frac{46}{200} = 0.23$.

mistakes.why: That divides by the 800 simulated children. A trial is a family, so divide by the 200 families.
That is 3 girls out of 4 children, the result being counted, not its estimated chance.

items.q: A student council of 8 seniors and 12 juniors says it picked 4 members at random to go to a conference, and all 4 chosen were seniors. In 100 simulated random picks of 4 members, only 2 picked 4 seniors. Build a conclusion about the claim.

why.correct: The estimated chance of 4 seniors in a random pick is $\frac{2}{100} = 0.02$. A result that rare gives reason to doubt that the pick was random, though it does not rule chance out.

evidence.label: Estimate
options: The estimated chance of 4 seniors in a random pick is about 0.02
The estimated chance of 4 seniors in a random pick is about 0.4
The chance of 4 seniors is 4 out of 20, or 0.2

why.1: 0.4 is the share of the council who are seniors (8 of 20), not the chance that all 4 picks are seniors.
why.2: Use the simulation: 2 of 100 trials, about 0.02.

claim.label: Conclusion
options: so a random pick rarely gives 4 seniors, which gives reason to doubt the pick was random
so the pick was certainly not random
so 4 seniors is a typical result of a random pick

why.1: Rare is not impossible: 2 of 100 random picks did give 4 seniors.
why.2: Only 2 of 100 trials gave 4 seniors, which is rare, not typical.

conclude.model: In the simulation only 2 of 100 random picks chose 4 seniors, an estimated chance of about 0.02. Because getting 4 seniors by chance is so unusual, this gives reason to doubt that the council picked the members at random.

items.q: Put the steps of a simulation in order.
options: Describe how one trial will be done with a chance device that has the right chances
Say what will be recorded at the end of each trial
Carry out many trials and record each result
Estimate the chance as the share of trials that gave the result

why.correct: Model the chance process, say what to record, repeat many times, then estimate with the share of trials. A plan someone else could follow names the device and its assignment first.

items.q: To simulate a 1-in-6 chance, a student lets the random digits 1 to 6 mean a success and 0, 7, 8 and 9 mean a failure. What is wrong with this plan?

why.correct: Each digit has a 1-in-10 chance, so 6 digits give a 6-in-10 chance of success, not 1 in 6. A fair die with one face as a success works, or the digits 1 to 6 with 0, 7, 8 and 9 skipped and the digit 1 as the success.
options: The digits come from 0 to 9, so the faces of a die are 6 of 10 equally common digits.
Right: 6 of the 10 digits are successes.
The number of digits is not the issue; the share of success digits is.
Adding 0 makes it 7 in 10, further from 1 in 6.
Nothing is wrong, since 1 to 6 are the faces of a die
It gives success a 6-in-10 chance, not a 1-in-6 chance
It should use 2-digit numbers, because 6 is a 1-digit number
The digit 0 should have been counted as a success, too
